newsitem.title: USA: Right engine becomes focus in Michigan plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Right engine becomes focus in Michigan plane crash.

text.p: Federal investigators chopped through ice and frozen mud at the Delta Comair crater Monday to excavate the plane's engines in search of reasons for why it crashed, killing 29 people.
Investigators want to know why cockpit levers indicated that pilots of Flight 3272 apparently took steps last Thursday to shut down the right engine and activate a fire extinguishing system.
"They'll be looking at that right engine," said National Transportation Safety Board spokesman Paul Schlamm.
The fiery crash in rural Monroe County, Mich., about 25 miles (40 km) south of Detroit Metropolitan Airport, ended a commuter flight from Cincinnati to Detroit.
On Monday night, investigators released their latest findings from the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder, which indicate the flight was normal until about 38 seconds before the crash.
The data released on Monday show that about 17 seconds before the crash, the plane experienced a rapid upset in roll and pitch and the autopilot disengaged.
A steep descent developed with several more steep roll and pitch oscillations. During the plane movements, the crew made no comments about the engine or system, investigators said.

In addition, cockpit controls showed the right propeller had been "feathered" to reduce aerodynamic drag, NTSB board member John Hammerschmidt said Sunday, adding that controls for the left engine were in normal operating position.
Feathering is a technique of changing the angle of propellor blades to lessen air resistance when an engine is idling or shut off.
Although the propellers had not been recovered, wreckage showed evidence that they were rotating at the time of impact, Schlamm said.
Monroe County Medical Examiner David Lieberman said late Monday that the remains of nearly all of the victims had been identified and were being turned over to their families.

Schlamm said the investigators also began to decontaminate and move pieces of wreckage from the crash site into a building at the nearby Monroe County Fairgrounds, where they will try to reconstruct the Brazilian-made Embraer commuter plane.
But frigid weather conditions were making it difficult for workers to extract pieces of the aircraft.
"They have to get through that frozen ground and ice without damaging the wreckage," Schlamm said.

In addition to examining the Pratt & Whitney engines, investigators also were continuing to probe the possibility that icing contributed to the crash. About 20 minutes after the crash, the pilot of a DC-3 aircraft reported icing in the same vicinity.
NTSB officials said they expected to wrap up most on-site work by the end of the week. Hammerschmidt, the lead investigator, returned to Washington Monday. He was to direct the probe from there.
